meta.title: Who really said "Money is like muck, not good except it be spread"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Francis Bacon really wrote it — essay XV, “Of Seditions and Troubles,” in his 1625 Essayes. The “money is like manure” versions came centuries later.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Money is like muck, not good except it be spread'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Francis Bacon, “Of Seditions and Troubles,” essay XV in the Essayes of 1625. Not King James I, not Thornton Wilder, not a Texas oilman.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The line is genuinely Bacon’s. It appears in essay XV, “Of Seditions and Troubles,” in The Essayes or Counsels, Civill and Morall (London, 1625) — the final, 58-essay edition published the year before he died. Quote Investigator, which traced the whole “muck” family of sayings, credits Bacon with the statement and cites the 1625 printing via Early English Books Online.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Of Seditions and Troubles,” essay XV, in The Essayes or Counsels, Civill and Morall
1625, London — the final, 58-essay edition, a year before Bacon’s death
Written in English — no translation involved

source.excerpt: Above all things, good Policie is to be used, that the Treasure and Moneyes in a State be not gathered into few Hands. For otherwise, a State may have a great Stock and yet starve. And Money is like Muck, not good except it be spread. This is done, chiefly, by suppressing, or, at the least, keeping a strait Hand upon the Devouring Trades of Usurie, Ingrossing, great Pasturages, and the like.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ is the anchor: it traced the whole “muck” family of sayings and credits Francis Bacon with this statement in his 1625 essay collection, reporting that it consulted The Essayes or Counsels, Ciuill and Morall of 1625 through Early English Books Online.
The sentence is present in context in the Wikisource text of the essay ↗, in Alfred S. West’s 1908 edition, inside Bacon’s list of remedies against sedition.
Wikiquote’s sourced list for the Essays ↗ files the line under “Of Seditions and Troubles” in the 1625 edition, and the quotation database WIST ↗ independently cites it as Essays, No. 15 (1625).

Bacon’s Essays grew across three editions — ten pieces in 1597, thirty-eight in 1612 and fifty-eight in 1625, per Wikipedia’s account of his life and work ↗. The 1625 edition is the one every citation for this line points to.

source.rightsNote: The essay was first published in London in 1625, in Bacon’s lifetime and in his own English — no translator sits between him and the reader. A work published four centuries ago is firmly in the public domain in the United States. Editorial apparatus in a modern reprint (introductions, notes, glossaries) may still be protected, but Bacon’s sentence is not.

author.name: Francis Bacon
author.heading: Who was Francis Bacon?
author.metaLine: 1561–1626 · Lord Chancellor of England, philosopher & essayist
author.bio: Francis Bacon, 1st Viscount St Alban (22 January 1561 – 9 April 1626), was an English philosopher and statesman who served as Attorney General and then Lord Chancellor of England before falling from office in 1621. He is best remembered as an architect of the empirical, experimental approach to knowledge that became the scientific method. His Essays grew across three editions — ten pieces in 1597, thirty-eight in 1612, and fifty-eight in the 1625 edition that contains this sentence.

misattribution.heading: The credit goes wandering
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Bacon is correct — but this is one of those sentences that keeps getting re-worded and re-assigned. Here is where the credit has drifted.

items.why: Twenty-five years after Bacon printed it, a collection titled Regales Aphorismi: or a Royal Chain of Golden Sentences presented “money is like muck, not good, unless it be spread” as a saying of James I. Quote Investigator documents the 1650 volume ↗.

items.who: Thornton Wilder and Clint Murchison Sr.
items.why: The barnyard word modernised and the credit moved. Quote Investigator records “Money is like manure of no use until it be spread” already in print in The New-Yorker in 1836; then LIFE in 1956 quoting Wilder’s play The Matchmaker — “money is like manure; it’s not worth a thing unless it’s spread around” — and TIME in 1961 giving a version to oilman Clint Murchison Sr. via his son. QI’s reading is that these modern figures used an existing saying rather than coining one. See the timeline ↗.

items.scope: The longer “riches are like muck” version
items.who: Bacon himself — but he credited a “Mr. Bettenham”
items.why: The expanded stinking-heap-versus-fruitful-field form is routinely quoted as Bacon’s own coinage. In his 1625 Apophthegmes New and Old he attributes it to Mr. Bettenham: “Riches were like Mucke…” Quote Investigator quotes the apophthegm ↗.

Sharing a name with a Jacobean Lord Chancellor is a liability. The other Francis Bacon (28 October 1909 – 28 April 1992 ↗) was an Irish-born British figurative painter, born long after this sentence was printed.

misattribution.truthLine: The short, sharp version — “Money is like muck, not good except it be spread” — is Bacon’s own, from “Of Seditions and Troubles” ↗ in the Essayes of 1625.

context.heading: Why Bacon said it
lead: The sentence is not a personal-finance maxim — it is a piece of statecraft. Bacon is listing the remedies a ruler should use against sedition, and the one he puts “above all things” is preventing wealth from pooling in a few hands. A country can be rich on paper and hungry in practice: “a State may have a great Stock and yet starve.”

The image is agricultural and deliberately unglamorous. Muck — dung — is worthless piled in a yard and valuable only once it is carted out and spread across a field. Bacon’s policy prescription follows immediately: keep “a strait Hand” on usury, engrossing and great pasturages, the practices he blamed for concentrating wealth.
context.detailsSummary: The longer version Bacon credited to someone else
detailsBody: In the same year, 1625, Bacon published Apophthegmes New and Old, which contains an expanded form of the same image — and Bacon there credits it not to himself but to a “Mr. Bettenham”: “Riches were like Mucke: When it lay, vpon an heape, it gaue but a stench…but when it was spread vpon the ground, then it was cause of much fruit.” That two-part version is the ancestor of the later proverb about riches stinking in a heap but making the earth fruitful when spread abroad. See Quote Investigator’s survey of the family ↗.
So the compact sentence in the Essays is Bacon’s own phrasing; the longer, stinking-heap version he presented as somebody else’s saying.
